source.title: Train-by-Reconnect: Decoupling Locations of Weights from Their Values

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including the appendix.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains networks by changing weight locations through permutation and reports training accuracy on CIFAR-10; this bears conceptually on whether training reaches low training error, though it does not use ordinary gradient training alone.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CIFAR-10 training-accuracy curves for LaPerm and comparisons with Adam and Lookahead. MNIST results and cited findings are excluded because they do not test a listed version; reported accuracy values visible only in figures are recorded as figure only. Descriptions of cited prior work are not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The ordinary Adam comparator reports CIFAR-10 training accuracy from random initialization, bearing directly on V1, including its qualification for regularized recipes. LaPerm's permutation-training results do not themselves test ordinary gradient training. The supplied text does not expose the comparator's numerical training accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that weight locations encode much of learned information and demonstrate training by reconnection, while retaining a gradient-based lookahead optimizer. They regard exact weight values as useful for final performance and restrict their experimental claims to classification on small vision datasets.
record.recipe_differences: LaPerm uses a regular gradient-based inner optimizer to look ahead, then permutes weights to reconnect them; it does not use ordinary gradient updates as the sole training intervention. Experiments are vision classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10, not the listed claim recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Sync period k changes training and validation accuracy trends; initialization distribution affects LaPerm performance; random pruning level affects performance, with severe drops at p ≥ 90%; learning-rate drops are associated with sharp ResNet50 accuracy increases.

fits_no_version.finding: LaPerm's synchronization period affects convergence and final accuracy, and reconnection preserves competitive CIFAR-10 accuracy across substantial random pruning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Permutation-based training performance depends on synchronization period and pruning level.

fits_no_version.finding: Shared-weight networks achieve approximately 85.5% and 53% MNIST accuracy; changing layerwise pruning raises the latter result to 78.14%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reconnection can train shared-weight networks, with performance depending on architecture and pruning allocation.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems, 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
record.problems: Most CIFAR-10 training-accuracy values are presented only in figures and not numerically stated. The paper uses LaPerm, which combines a gradient-based lookahead optimizer with a distinct permutation intervention, so results do not establish the ordinary gradient-training claims in the listed versions. Some settings select synchronization periods based on performance or non-divergence, and the text notes instability in ResNet50 before learning-rate drops.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only plotted results were retained where the text reports a relevant training-accuracy outcome or curve, without estimating numeric values from plots.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD, systematic model-size and early-stopping comparisons, and whether the unreadable Adam curves reach zero or near-zero training error.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Matched depth comparisons with and without identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and Fixup.

Initialization effects on training speed, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth. Section 5.1 compares LaPerm validation accuracy across initializations, which does not establish these effects.
Initial stability thresholds, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to measured thresholds.
Matched training-speed and learning-rate-tolerance comparisons with and without batch normalization, and Fixup. Resetting learned BN affine parameters retains normalization.

missing.what: The unpruned ResNet50 ordinary Adam comparator's training-accuracy curve should be recorded separately. It bears on V1, but its numerical values are unavailable in the supplied text, preventing a directional verdict.

record.verdict_notes: No directional verdict is justified by the readable evidence linked to V1. The unreadable Adam training curves warrant cannot_determine, rather than support or challenge. LaPerm comparisons, initialization-dependent validation accuracy, scheduled learning-rate recovery, and BN affine-parameter resets do not by themselves test the other versions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test ordinary SGD or Adam from random initialization for zero or near-zero training classification error, corrupted or random labels, or comparisons involving smaller models and early stopping. LaPerm uses gradient-based updates for lookahead but changes weights by permutation.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or width comparison of student and teacher is tested.
No depth comparison of plain and residual networks tests the listed shortcut claim.
The paper does not compare initialization schemes for signal propagation, trainable depth, or orthogonal versus Gaussian weights.
No learning-rate stability threshold, loss-rise/collapse, or sharpness measurement is tested.
Batch normalization is used in some experiments, but no matched comparison tests whether it speeds training or improves learning-rate tolerance; Fixup is not tested.
